nodes.title: Community Awareness
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe their community, identify the people and places in it, and explain the roles community members play.

nodes.title: Local Geography
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe the physical and human features of their local area and locate familiar places on a simple map.

nodes.title: Local History
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe how their local community has changed over time using stories, artifacts, and firsthand accounts.

nodes.title: National Symbols & Identity
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can identify major national symbols, holidays, and pledges and explain what they represent.

nodes.title: Early Civilizations
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe key features of early human civilizations, including agriculture, settlements, and early government.

nodes.title: World Geography
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can locate the continents, oceans, and major countries and describe the world's major physical regions.

nodes.title: World History Overview
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can outline the broad sequence of major world eras and civilizations from ancient times to the present.

nodes.title: Cause & Effect in History
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can identify the causes and effects of a historical event and explain how they are connected.

nodes.title: Primary & Secondary Sources
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can distinguish primary from secondary sources and use evidence from a source to answer a historical question.

nodes.title: Government Basics
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain the basic purpose of government and identify the main functions it performs for society.

nodes.title: Citizenship & Responsibility
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe the rights and responsibilities of a good citizen and give examples of responsible civic behavior.

nodes.title: Economics Basics
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how people meet needs and wants through producing, exchanging, and consuming goods and services.

nodes.title: Global Interactions
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how trade, communication, and migration connect nations and cultures around the world.

nodes.title: Historical Analysis
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can analyze a historical event using multiple sources, weighing evidence and perspective to build an interpretation.

nodes.title: Political Systems
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can compare major political systems and explain how power is organized and exercised in each.

nodes.title: Modern Issues & Society
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can analyze a contemporary social issue using historical context and multiple perspectives.

nodes.title: Civic Engagement
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can plan and carry out an informed civic action that addresses a real community or public issue.

nodes.title: Leadership & Influence
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can evaluate how leaders influence groups and demonstrate leadership by guiding a collaborative effort.

nodes.title: US History
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can outline the major periods of United States history and place key events in chronological order.

nodes.title: Comparative History
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can compare developments across two or more societies or eras and explain their similarities and differences.

nodes.title: Geopolitics
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can analyze how geography, resources, and power shape relationships and conflicts among nations.

nodes.title: Advanced Economics
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can apply economic models to analyze markets, policy, and trade-offs at national and global scales.

nodes.title: Law & Justice
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how laws are made and applied and evaluate a case in terms of rights, fairness, and justice.

nodes.title: Cultural Studies
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe the elements of a culture and compare beliefs, customs, and values across different cultures.

nodes.title: Reading Maps
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can locate places and follow directions on a simple map of a familiar area.

nodes.title: Map Keys, Scale & Compass
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can use a map key, scale bar, and compass rose to read symbols, distance, and direction on a map.

nodes.title: Latitude & Longitude
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can use lines of latitude and longitude to locate a place by its coordinates.

nodes.title: Physical vs Political Maps
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can distinguish physical from political maps and explain what each type of map shows.

nodes.title: Regions
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can group places into regions based on shared physical or human characteristics.

nodes.title: Human-Environment Interaction
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how people adapt to, modify, and depend on their physical environment.

nodes.title: Migration
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe why people migrate and how migration changes both origin and destination places.

nodes.title: Native Peoples & Pre-Columbian America
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe the diverse Native American cultures that existed in the Americas before European contact.

nodes.title: Colonization of America
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain why Europeans colonized the Americas and describe daily life in the early colonies.

nodes.title: American Revolution
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain the causes of the American Revolution and how the colonies won their independence.

nodes.title: Constitution & Founding
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe how the US Constitution was created and the principles the new government was founded on.

nodes.title: Westward Expansion
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe US westward expansion and its effects on settlers and Native peoples.

nodes.title: Civil War & Reconstruction
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain the causes of the Civil War and the goals and outcomes of Reconstruction.

nodes.title: Industrialization
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe how industrialization transformed the US economy, cities, and workforce.

nodes.title: Civil Rights Movement
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain the goals, key events, and outcomes of the Civil Rights Movement.

nodes.title: 20th-Century US History
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can outline major 20th-century US events, including the World Wars, the Great Depression, and the postwar era.

nodes.title: Classical Empires
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe major classical empires such as Greece, Rome, and Han China and their lasting contributions.

nodes.title: Middle Ages
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe life, power, and religion in the medieval world across several regions.

nodes.title: Renaissance
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how the Renaissance renewed art, learning, and science in Europe.

nodes.title: Age of Exploration
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe the motives and consequences of European overseas exploration and the resulting global exchange.

nodes.title: Revolutions
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain the causes and effects of major political and industrial revolutions.

nodes.title: World Wars
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain the causes, course, and consequences of the two World Wars.

nodes.title: Modern World
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe major developments in the world since 1945, including the Cold War and globalization.

nodes.title: The Constitution
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain the structure and purpose of the US Constitution and how it organizes and limits government.

nodes.title: Bill of Rights
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can identify the rights protected by the Bill of Rights and give an everyday example of each.

nodes.title: Three Branches of Government
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can name the three branches of government and describe the role and powers of each.

nodes.title: Federalism & Levels of Government
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can distinguish local, state, and federal government and explain how powers are divided among them.

nodes.title: Types of Government
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can compare types of government such as democracy, monarchy, and dictatorship.

nodes.title: Voting & Elections
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how elections work and why voting is central to a democracy.

nodes.title: Needs vs Wants
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can distinguish between needs and wants and sort everyday examples of each.

nodes.title: Goods & Services
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can distinguish goods from services and identify who produces and who consumes them.

nodes.title: Money & Trade
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how money makes trade easier than barter and how people exchange goods and services.

nodes.title: Scarcity & Choice
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain scarcity and describe the trade-offs and opportunity cost of a choice.

nodes.title: Supply & Demand
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how supply and demand interact to set the price of a good.

nodes.title: Markets
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how markets coordinate buyers and sellers and how competition affects prices and choices.

nodes.title: Personal Finance & Budgeting
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can build a simple budget and explain saving, spending, and the cost of borrowing.

nodes.title: World Religions
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can identify the major world religions and describe a core belief and practice of each.

nodes.title: Cultural Diffusion
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how ideas, goods, and customs spread between cultures through contact and exchange.

nodes.title: Traditions & Values
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe traditions and shared values in a culture and compare them with their own.

nodes.title: Diversity
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can describe the diversity of people within a community and explain why respecting differences matters.

nodes.title: Current Events Analysis
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can analyze a current news event, identify its sources, and explain multiple perspectives on it.

nodes.title: Chronology & Timelines
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can place events in order on a timeline and use terms like past, present, and future correctly.

nodes.title: Sequencing Events
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can sequence a series of historical events in the correct order and describe what came before and after.

nodes.title: Point of View & Bias
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can identify the author's point of view in a source and explain how bias can shape an account.

nodes.title: Historical Context
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can explain how the context of a time period shaped the events and decisions within it.

nodes.title: Continuity & Change
nodes.mastery_criteria: Student can identify what stayed the same and what changed across a period of history.

merges.note: SS19 US History was a single coarse node covering all of US history. Retained as the survey/base atomic (chronological overview) and decomposed into the standard era atomics: Native peoples -> Colonization -> Revolution -> Constitution -> Westward Expansion -> Civil War/Reconstruction -> Industrialization -> Civil Rights -> 20th century. Original junk edge SS7->SS19 (world-history overview hard-locking US history) dropped; SS19 now anchors on SS3/SS9 (soft). Original SS19->SS14 leads_to dropped in favor of SS14's own source/cause prereqs.

SS7 World History Overview was a single coarse node. Retained as the survey/base atomic and decomposed into era atomics: Classical Empires -> Middle Ages -> Renaissance -> Age of Exploration -> Revolutions -> World Wars -> Modern World. Ancient civilizations remain covered by existing SS5 (SS7 now hard-depends on SS5). Original junk chain SS6->SS7->SS8 dropped; cause&effect (SS8) no longer requires the world-history survey.

SS10 Government Basics was a single coarse node. Retained as the base atomic and decomposed into: The Constitution, Bill of Rights, Three Branches, Federalism & Levels of Government, Types of Government, Voting & Elections. Original junk edges SS9->SS10 (sources hard-locking government) and SS10->SS11 (government before citizenship, inverted grade bands) converted to soft; SS11 Citizenship moved earlier (Fluency, 3-6).

SS12 Economics Basics was a single coarse node. Retained as the base atomic; the concrete concepts split out: Needs vs Wants, Goods & Services, Money & Trade (elementary feeders) plus Scarcity & Choice, Supply & Demand, Markets, Personal Finance & Budgeting. Original junk edge SS11->SS12 (citizenship hard-locking economics, cross-strand) dropped; SS12 now built on the money/trade feeders. Advanced Economics (SS22) re-anchored on SS-345 Markets instead of the old SS12->SS22 hard lock.

SS6 World Geography was coarse. Retained as the base atomic; the map/spatial skills SS-301..SS-303 (Reading Maps, Map Keys/Scale/Compass, Latitude & Longitude) added as new foundational feeders BELOW it, and the thematic geography SS-304..SS-307 (Physical vs Political, Regions, Human-Environment Interaction, Migration) split out from it. Original junk chain SS5->SS6->SS7 replaced: SS6 now hard-depends on map skills (SS-302), soft on SS2/SS5.

Coverage: C3/NCSS 'sourcing & evidence' is covered by existing SS9 Primary & Secondary Sources (not duplicated). SS-362 Point of View & Bias added alongside it as a distinct skill. SS9's original hard-lock on SS8 relaxed to soft so sources can be taught independently of cause & effect.

Coverage: 'rights & responsibilities of citizens' is covered by existing SS11 Citizenship & Responsibility; not duplicated as a new node. SS11 was relocated from the middle of the junk linear spine to a Fluency (grade 3-6) civic-foundations skill feeding SS17 Civic Engagement.
Coverage: 'ancient civilizations' is covered by existing SS5 Early Civilizations; SS-320 Classical Empires added as the next World-History era rather than duplicating ancient civ.

Structural fix: the original graph was a single linear hard-prereq spine SS1->SS2->...->SS18 plus 6 branch nodes, with 23 hard edges and 0 soft edges, forcing (e.g.) Local Geography before Local History, National Symbols before Early Civilizations, and Government before Economics. That spine was dismantled. Cross-strand locks were converted to soft_deps and directions corrected (local before world; foundations before advanced; concept before application). Hard prereqs are now retained only within a strand's genuine build order.
